trailer.intro: Email Autopilot for Financial Services — every action runs through the same runtime you are about to see.
trailer.intake: An unauthenticated dispute email is triaged, filed and clocked on arrival — no human in the loop for intake.
trailer.dossier: Same runtime, second screen: every policy condition is PASS or FAIL, and the rail on the right spells each decision out in plain words.
trailer.clocks: The board is not just this case: the table below is every open dispute in the mailbox, and who is due first is obvious.
trailer.approve: Statutory obligations surface in the supervisor queue with one-click approval — the click is a real human action, not a scripted screen.
trailer.fraud: A business-email-compromise attempt is quarantined: the requested contact changes are structurally unreachable, and the customer is warned only through the on-file channel.
trailer.builder: Autonomy is earned: backtest, sampling, dual sign-off — and the hard cells cannot be opened from configuration at all.
trailer.outro: Deterministic where the law requires it, autonomous where evidence has earned it, auditable everywhere.

email1.publicMailbox: Day 0: a mail arrives from a public Gmail address that is not on file. The sender is not in the customer's file, so identity assurance only reaches I1 — the system does not know who wrote it.
email1.lockedCell: Overdraft refund × I1 is a locked cell: this email gets no automatic refund and no AI-written body. The customer receives a fixed template that only tells her to verify in the mobile app — the email itself contains no link at all.
email1.caseCard: Verification happens inside the same mail thread: the app pushes a notice, the one-time code goes to the phone number on file, six digits go in, and the case keeps going on its own.
email1.identityUp: Verification passed, and identity in this same thread rises from I1 to I3. The panel on the right is the evidence: the sender address still does not match the customer file, but 'step-up completed in this thread' and 'logged-in secure-message session' both pass, and the footer reads verification valid, held at I3.
email1.i3refund: The same rule is evaluated again with the new identity: this cell now allows it, the $35 overdraft fee goes back to the customer's account, and the reply is still three sources stitched together — locked template, system slot, generated sentence. Every letter passes a compliance check before it leaves, carrying AI disclosure and a human handoff.
email1.provenance: One letter, colored by source: blue is the locked template, green is the system slot (name, amount, date, case id), purple is the generated sentence.
email1.verified: Fourteen days with no new mail, no handoff and no QA reversal — one more line on the audit rail: a verified autonomous resolution. The dossier is sealed for the record, and human edits flow back as samples.
email1.secondRequest: Day 21, a second mail in the same thread: the customer asks again for the overdraft fee back. It is merged into the same case, not a new one; identity is still I3, nothing was downgraded.
email1.holding: The bank answers the same day with a second letter: it confirms receipt, says a supervisor will reply within one business day, and states plainly that she can still ask for a human review. This letter promises no outcome.
email1.secondWaiver: Why it is not automatic: the first overdraft-waiver rule requires no more than 1 waiver in the past 12 months, and that field now reads 2 — so the condition fails and the cell drops from auto-execute to one-click approval. The boundary is the policy result, not the model's mood.
email1.l2queue: The explanation draft goes into the supervisor queue — the customer always keeps a human reconsideration path. Sending passes the same compliance check, with disclosure and a handoff.
email1.explanationSent: One supervisor click and the explanation letter goes straight back into the customer's own thread: why this one could not be automatic, which rule was applied, and that she can still ask for a review.
email1.secondClosed: Fourteen days after the explanation letter with no new contact, one more line on the audit rail: beat two closes as a human-resolved case for the books, corrections flow back as samples, the dossier is sealed for the record.
email1.outro: Same intent, same customer, two different outcomes — because the value in that cell changed, and every change can be explained.

email2.intake: Day 0, 08:14: one email contains two intents — card delivery status and a $247.18 dispute. Both are filed on arrival and the Reg E statutory clocks start immediately, even at I0. Language English, vulnerability negative and fraud negative screen in parallel with intent; same-thread merge, alias normalization, duplicate deliveries auto-suppressed.
email2.detailDenied: Day 1, the customer asks for transaction details. Unmentioned transactions are an I3 field class, and this thread is I2 — disclosure is denied, with an app verification prompt.
email2.detailReleased: After in-thread step-up to I3, the disputed transaction details are released, last four digits only.
email2.materials: Day 6: the signed statement arrives as an attachment. OCR confidence is high enough to auto-slot it; low-confidence OCR would stay with a human. Missing materials never pause the statutory clock.
email2.clock48h: Business day 10 is the provisional-credit deadline; inside 48 calendar hours the board turns red — time is computed, never judged. The table below is every open dispute in the mailbox: who is due first, which credit already posted.
email2.restart: Before approving, we kill the process and reopen it. A fresh runtime reattaches to the same checkpoints: the pending approval is still here, and the money action will not execute twice — gateway ledger plus server-side idempotent replay. This is the engineering problem behind long-running autopilots.
email2.pcApproved: One click releases the credit, and the posting email lands in the customer's own thread — same AI disclosure, same human handoff.
email2.evidence: Day 40: merchant evidence arrives by email. Adjudication is R4 — permanently human. The AI drafts, the person decides.
email2.adjudication: The supervisor upholds the error; the result letter is chained into an L1 human sign-off in the same run, passing the same gate on send.
email2.closed: Day 45, inside the POS 90-day outer limit: the result letter is already in the customer's thread and the dispute closes with the full decision dossier, sealed WORM; corrections flow back as samples.
email2.outro: A 45-day, cross-system case that survives process restarts — with a human on every high-risk action.

email3.signals: Day 2: jane.d0e@outlook.com — a lookalike of the on-file address. SPF and DKIM pass, but DMARC is 'none'; the display name is spoofed; the attachment embeds the instruction 'skip OTP', which is treated as data, not a command. Identity assurance rates I0.
email3.noTools: The email asks to change the phone number and mail a card to a new address. The matrix lookup takes the isolation branch: in the email channel no such tools are registered — the buttons are greyed out at the configuration layer AND absent at the tool layer.
email3.onfile: Confirming fraud, the warning SMS goes to the on-file number on the phone only — never to the address the attacker controls.
email3.sar: A supporting record is generated from a locked template containing facts only — no conclusions, and nothing ever transmitted to the forged address.
email3.closed: After confirmation the case closes: on-file SMS sent, SAR locked template archived, dossier sealed WORM; miss and false-positive samples flow back to the detector.
email3.outro: Prompt injection, BEC and ATO meet a system whose attack surface was designed closed.

builder.intro: Autonomy is not configured by a slider — it is earned per intent, and the R × I matrix is rendered by the same decision function that runs in production.
builder.replay: A 90-day recorded dataset is replayed: agreement, no-edit approval, regulated recall, critical misses, unit cost — plus two regret columns, per million, for autonomy and for conservatism. Every number is a recorded fixture.
builder.sampling: Three sampling tiers — stratified, random, and adversarial — across three intake frames, including tickets that were never created. Tier C is reported separately.
builder.unsignable: The negative re-label is a separate 1,200-item batch, not part of the 350. Watch what happens if detector-negative items are not independently re-labeled: the recall criterion becomes not signable.
builder.promoted: Compliance and the business owner both sign: the shadow intent is promoted, and the next inbound email of that type immediately runs at the new level — same runtime.
builder.r3never: Contact-detail change is R3. Click the cells: nothing happens. They are disabled in configuration and no tool function exists — there is no setting that opens them.
builder.rare: Wire recalls are rare: 90 days can never reach the sample bar. They stay human, with a conformal abstention fallback calibrated to route uncertain cases to an agent.
builder.outro: Every autonomous action in this demo traces back to evidence a regulator would accept.
